question:
Patient note:
A 41-year-old woman arrived to the infectious-disease clinic from a local shelter complaining of progressively worsening exertional breathlessness and morning productive cough over the past two months, superimposed upon longstanding baseline respiratory limitations dating back almost a decade. She reports a 22 pack-year cigarette history that she has cut down to five cigarettes daily and admits frequent second-hand smoke exposure in communal living spaces. Pulmonology notes from three years earlier documented a post-bronchodilator FEV1 of 64 % predicted and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.57, consistent with moderate fixed airflow obstruction; she was started at that time on twice-daily budesonide–formoterol and as-needed albuterol, which she continues to use, though more often recently. She denies ever needing home oxygen, intubation, or non-invasive ventilation, yet concedes two emergency-department visits in the past year for bronchitic flares treated with short oral corticosteroid tapers. In addition to her pulmonary concerns, she has a twelve-year history of human immunodeficiency virus infection complicated by a nadir CD4 lymphocyte count of 148 cells/mm³ and an episode of oropharyngeal candidiasis four years ago. She had been virologically suppressed on a bictegravir-based single-tablet regimen but ran out of medication three months ago when insurance lapsed; a point-of-care test today shows an HIV-1 RNA of 184,000 copies/mL, and her most recent CD4 count drawn two weeks earlier at a community program was 182 cells/mm³. She recalls no episodes of Kaposi sarcoma, Pneumocystis pneumonia, cryptococcal meningitis, or other severe opportunistic processes. Her liver enzymes have been mildly elevated since her twenties, and she was found to have chronic hepatitis C genotype 1a with low-grade fibrosis by non-invasive elastography (liver stiffness 6.1 kPa). She abstains from alcohol, has never shown stigmata of portal hypertension, maintains a normal bilirubin, and her last abdominal ultrasound six months ago demonstrated preserved hepatic architecture without nodularity or ascites. She was counselled to defer direct-acting antiviral therapy until her antiretrovirals were re-established but otherwise remains clinically compensated. She underwent screening laboratory tests at the shelter that showed fasting glucose values between 98 and 108 mg/dL; a contemporaneous hemoglobin A1c was 6.6 %, and she was formally diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus that is presently managed with diet and lifestyle modification alone. Nutrition staff have implemented a lower-carbohydrate meal plan, and she has not required hypoglycemic agents nor developed neuropathic, retinal, or renal sequelae. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, pedal edema, or prior coronary interventions. She is able to climb half a flight of stairs before pausing to catch her breath but attributes the limitation to wheeze rather than cardiac discomfort. She has no calf cramps on walking, no history of limb ulcers, and intact peripheral pulses were documented at her last primary-care visit. She also denies focal neurologic deficits, speech disturbances, vision loss, or episodes suggestive of transient ischemia; cognition remains sharp, and she continues to manage her personal paperwork and medications independently. She has no rheumatologic diagnoses, no history of malar rash, photosensitivity, or serositis, and has never been treated with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. She reports no dyspepsia, hematemesis, or melena, and has never undergone esophagogastroduodenoscopy. She drinks two cups of coffee daily, uses no illicit drugs, and has been off alcohol entirely for six years. Surgical history is limited to a tubal ligation at age 30. Current medications include the aforementioned inhalers, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole 800/160 mg once daily for infection prophylaxis, a daily multivitamin, and as-needed ibuprofen for musculoskeletal aches; she is not on corticosteroids chronically, anticoagulants, or statins. Family history is notable only for maternal type 2 diabetes diagnosed late in life; there is no premature coronary disease, stroke, or malignancy on either side. On presentation today she appears thin but in no acute distress, speaking in full sentences with occasional end-expiratory wheeze. Vital signs: temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg in the right arm seated, pulse 88 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 95 % on room air which drops to 92 % with minimal ambulation in the corridor. Body mass index is 23 kg/m². Pulmonary examination reveals decreased breath sounds bilaterally with diffuse polyphonic wheezes, no crackles, and no dullness to percussion. Cardiac auscultation shows a normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; jugular venous pressure is not elevated. Abdomen is soft, non-tender, with the liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin but smooth and non-nodular, and there is no splenomegaly or flank dullness. Extremities demonstrate warm, well-perfused skin without edema or clubbing; distal pulses are 2+ and symmetrical. Neurologic exam is non-focal, and gait is steady. Point-of-care fingerstick glucose is 104 mg/dL. Laboratory studies drawn this morning reveal hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 4.1 × 10⁹/L, platelets 168 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, BUN 12 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, AST 52 U/L, ALT 61 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 108 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, and albumin 4.0 g/dL. A 12-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 86 beats/min with no ST-segment deviations or pathologic Q-waves. Portable chest radiograph demonstrates hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms and no parenchymal infiltrates. Sputum culture and pulmonary function testing are being arranged, and social-work consultation has been requested to assist with reinstating insurance coverage for her antiretroviral regimen.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index adds weighted comorbidity points and, in the age-adjusted version, age points.
• Age 41: 0 points (under 50).
• AIDS: +6. Her documented CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ meets the AIDS criterion even without an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection.
• Chronic pulmonary disease: +1. Spirometry confirms persistent airflow obstruction requiring inhalers.
• Mild liver disease: +1. Chronic hepatitis C with low-grade fibrosis and no portal hypertension qualifies.
• Diabetes: 0. Diet-controlled diabetes without end-organ damage does not meet the classic CCI diabetes criterion.
• No other score-bearing comorbidities are documented: 0.
Total = 0 + 6 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 8.
Final answer: 8
